present.explain: A Spanish verb changes its ending for who does it. For verbs like tomar: tomo (I), tomas (you), toma (he, she, you polite), tomamos (we). For verbs like comer: como, comes, come, comemos. Some common verbs change more: tengo, tienes, tiene; quiero, quieres, quiere. English mostly adds -s for he and she; Spanish has a different ending for each person.
present.why: The ending carries the person. [[Tomo]] already means I drink, and [[tomas]] already means you drink, so the ending is the part to listen for: [[Ella toma]] té y [[yo tomo]] café.

examples.means: I drink coffee.
examples.literal: I drink coffee.

examples.means: Do you drink tea?
examples.literal: You drink tea?

examples.text: Mi mamá toma café con leche.
examples.means: My mom drinks coffee with milk.
examples.literal: My mom drinks coffee with milk.

examples.means: We eat here.
examples.literal: We eat here.

examples.text: Él tiene café y yo tengo té.
examples.means: He has coffee, and I have tea.
examples.literal: He has coffee and I have tea.

contrasts.says: Because the ending already says who, Spanish usually leaves out yo, tú and the rest.
After querer or poder the second verb keeps its basic form: quiero tomar, never quiero tomo.

mistakes.why: With yo the ending is -o.
For one person who isn't you or I, the ending is -a (or -e).

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons, open to correction.

no-subject.explain: Spanish usually leaves out the word for who does it, because the verb's ending already says it: Tomo café is I drink coffee. Say yo, tú, él, ella or nosotros when it matters who, to contrast two people or to make clear who you mean: Tú tomas café y yo tomo té.
no-subject.why: English needs I or you in every sentence; in Spanish the ending does that job, so [[Tomo]] café is complete. Adding yo where nothing contrasts sounds like stressing I: [[Yo]] tomo café, me, not you.

examples.means: I drink coffee.
examples.literal: I drink coffee.

examples.means: Are you OK?
examples.literal: Are you OK?

examples.text: Tú tomas café y yo tomo té.
examples.means: You drink coffee, and I drink tea.
examples.literal: You drink coffee and I drink tea.

examples.means: Is he coming home too?
examples.literal: He too comes home?

contrasts.says: The ending is what tells you who: tomo is I, tomas is you, toma is he or she.
English can't drop I or you; Spanish usually does.

mistakes.wrong: Yo tomo café, yo como bien.
mistakes.why: Repeating yo with nothing to contrast sounds heavy; the endings already say who.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons, open to correction.

gender.explain: Every Spanish noun is either an el word or a la word, and the words with it follow: el teléfono, un libro; la mesa, una llave. Many el words end in -o and many la words in -a, but not all (el café, la leche), so learn each noun with its el or la. A few la words that start with a stressed a take el and un in the singular: el agua, un agua.
gender.why: The noun decides, and the little words around it agree. Change the noun and [[el]] becomes [[la]], [[un]] becomes [[una]], [[mucho]] becomes [[mucha]]: mucho café, mucha agua.

examples.text: El teléfono está en la mesa.
examples.means: The phone is on the table.
examples.literal: The phone is on the table.

examples.means: I have the key.
examples.literal: I have the key.

examples.text: Un té con leche, por favor.
examples.means: A tea with milk, please.
examples.literal: A tea with milk, please.

examples.means: I drink a lot of water.
examples.literal: I drink a lot of water.

contrasts.says: English has one the and one a for every noun; Spanish has el or la, un or una, by the noun.
mi and tu are the same for el and la words: mi libro, mi llave.

mistakes.why: teléfono is an el word: learn it as el teléfono.
llave is a la word; learn it as la llave.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons, open to correction.

question.explain: A written question opens with an upside-down ¿ and closes with ?. A yes-or-no question can keep the order of a statement and just rise in tone: ¿El carro está aquí? After a question word like dónde, qué or cómo, the verb comes next, and the subject after it: ¿Dónde está el carro? Spanish never adds a word like English do.
question.why: The ¿ warns you a question is coming, so you hear it from the start. With a question word, the verb follows straight away: [[¿Dónde está]] el carro?, not ¿Dónde el carro está?

examples.means: Where's the car?
examples.literal: Where is the car?

examples.means: Do you drink coffee?
examples.literal: You drink coffee?

examples.means: What do you want to do?
examples.literal: What you want to do?

examples.means: Is the coffee here?
examples.literal: Is here the coffee?

contrasts.says: English adds do or does to most questions; Spanish doesn't, and puts the verb right after a question word.

mistakes.why: After dónde, the verb comes next.
A written question opens with ¿.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons, open to correction.

ser-estar.explain: Spanish has two verbs for to be. estar says where something or someone is (El libro está en la mesa) and how someone is right now (Estoy bien). ser says what something is (Es un libro) and whose it is (Es de mi mamá). For where a thing is, it's always estar.
ser-estar.why: Ask what you're saying. Where it is, or how someone is: [[está]], [[estoy]]. What it is, or whose: [[es]]. So the same phone is: Es mi teléfono (what it is), and Está en la mesa (where it is).

examples.text: El teléfono está en la mesa.
examples.means: The phone is on the table.
examples.literal: The phone is on the table.

examples.means: I'm fine, thanks.
examples.literal: I am fine, thanks.

examples.means: That's a book.
examples.literal: That is a book.

examples.text: El teléfono es de mi mamá.
examples.means: The phone is my mom's.
examples.literal: The phone is of my mom.

examples.means: It's my car.
examples.literal: It is my car.

contrasts.says: English uses is for all of these; Spanish chooses between es and está.
Whose something is takes ser and de: es de mi mamá.

mistakes.wrong: El teléfono es en la mesa.
mistakes.right: El teléfono está en la mesa.
mistakes.why: Where a thing is takes estar.
How you are takes estar.
What something is takes ser.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons, open to correction.

possessive.explain: mi (my) and tu (your, to someone you say tú to) go before the noun, and they're the same for el and la words: mi libro, mi llave, tu carro, tu casa. With a plural noun they add -s: mis llaves. su says his, her, its, their, and your to someone you say usted to.
possessive.why: Where English says my, Spanish puts [[mi]] in place of el or la: el libro becomes [[mi libro]], la llave becomes [[mi llave]]. Written with an accent, mí is a different word: me.

examples.means: Where's my key?
examples.literal: Where is my key?

examples.text: Mi teléfono está en mi bolsillo.
examples.means: My phone is in my pocket.
examples.literal: My phone is in my pocket.

examples.means: Is that one your dad's?
examples.literal: That one is of your dad?

examples.means: My car is here.
examples.literal: My car is here.

contrasts.says: el and la change with the noun; mi and tu don't.
For someone's, Spanish says de: el libro de mi mamá, my mom's book.

mistakes.why: mí with an accent is me; my is mi.
mi takes the place of la; they don't go together.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons, open to correction.

negation.explain: no goes right before the verb: No tomo café, Ella no viene, El café no está listo. Answering a question with no, the first no is the answer and the second goes before the verb: No, no tomo leche. There's no word like English do in it.
negation.why: English puts not after a helper (I do not drink); Spanish has no helper, so [[no]] goes straight before the verb: [[No tomo]] café.

examples.means: I don't drink coffee.
examples.literal: Not I drink coffee.

examples.means: She isn't coming.
examples.literal: She not comes.

examples.means: The coffee isn't ready.
examples.literal: The coffee not is ready.

examples.means: No, I don't drink milk.
examples.literal: No, not I drink milk.

contrasts.says: English adds do or does with not; Spanish just puts no before the verb.
A question with no keeps it before the verb too: ¿Tú no tomas café?

mistakes.why: no goes before the verb, not after it.
no goes before está.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons, open to correction.

modal.explain: After querer (want), poder (can) and tener que (have to), the next verb stays in its basic form, the one that ends in -ar, -er or -ir: Quiero comer, ¿Puedes leer eso?, Tengo que trabajar. Only the first verb changes for who does it. Nothing goes between them: no a, no to.
modal.why: One verb at a time takes the person's ending. [[Quiero]] already says I want, so the second stays plain: [[Quiero comer]], never quiero como.

examples.means: I want to have a coffee.
examples.literal: I want to have a coffee.

examples.means: Can you read that?
examples.literal: You can read that?

examples.means: I still have to work.
examples.literal: Still I have to work.

examples.text: Mi mamá quiere comer en casa.
examples.means: My mom wants to eat at home.
examples.literal: My mom wants to eat at home.

contrasts.says: The first verb takes the ending (quiero, quieres, quiere); the second never does.
English puts to between them (want to eat); Spanish puts nothing: quiero comer.

mistakes.why: After quiero, the basic form.
Nothing goes between querer and the next verb.
Have to is tener que, with que.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons, open to correction.

demonstrative.explain: esto (this) and eso (that) point at a thing you don't name: ¿Qué es esto?, Eso es un libro. este and ese go with a noun, or stand for one you could name, and match it: este libro, esa mesa, ese (that one). esto and eso never go before a noun.
demonstrative.why: Pointing at something you haven't named yet, use [[esto]] or [[eso]]: ¿Qué es [[eso]]? Once it's a book, it's ese libro, or just [[ese]], that one.

examples.means: What's this?
examples.literal: What is this?

examples.means: That's a book.
examples.literal: That is a book.

examples.means: This is for you.
examples.literal: This is for you.

examples.means: Is that one your dad's?
examples.literal: That one is of your dad?

contrasts.says: este and ese match their noun (esta, esa); esto and eso never change.

mistakes.why: Before a noun, este, never esto.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons, open to correction.

usted.explain: usted is the polite you, for someone you don't know well, someone older, or anyone you want to show respect to. Its verb takes the form for él and ella: ¿Usted sabe dónde está?, ¿Sabe usted qué es esto? After a word like para it stays usted: Esto es para usted.
usted.why: usted grew out of an old way of saying your grace, so it takes the verb of a third person: [[usted sabe]], like él sabe, never usted sabes.

examples.means: Do you know where my car is?
examples.literal: You know where is my car?

examples.means: Do you know what this is?
examples.literal: Know you what is this?

examples.means: This is for you.
examples.literal: This is for you.

contrasts.says: usted is said more often than tú, because sabe alone could also be he or she knows.
usted takes the él and ella ending: usted toma, usted quiere, usted tiene.

mistakes.why: usted takes the él and ella form.
After para, tú becomes ti; usted stays usted.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons, open to correction.

de.explain: de joins two nouns where English puts one before the other, and it says whose something is: la llave de mi carro (the key of my car: my car key), el libro de mi mamá (my mom's book), Es de mi mamá (it's my mom's). Spanish has no 's.
de.why: English says my mom's book; Spanish turns it round: el libro [[de]] mi mamá, the book of my mom.

examples.text: El teléfono es de mi mamá.
examples.means: The phone is my mom's.
examples.literal: The phone is of my mom.

examples.text: ¿Él tiene la llave de mi carro?
examples.means: Does he have the key to my car?
examples.literal: He has the key of my car?

examples.text: Entonces voy a casa de mi papá.
examples.means: Then I'll go to my dad's.
examples.literal: Then I go to house of my dad.

contrasts.says: Whose something is takes ser: es de mi mamá.
English uses 's or puts the nouns side by side; Spanish uses de.

mistakes.right: Es el libro de mi mamá.
mistakes.why: Spanish has no 's: the book of my mom.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons, open to correction.

hay.explain: hay introduces something present or available. It means there is with one thing and there are with more than one; hay itself does not change. Use it with a new or unspecified person or thing: Hay alguien en la puerta, Hay una puerta abierta. To locate a particular door already being discussed, use estar: La puerta está aquí.
hay.why: Spanish needs no separate word for there: [[Hay]] café is a complete sentence. In [[Hay alguien]] en la puerta, you introduce someone rather than locate a person already named.

examples.means: There's someone at the door.
examples.literal: There is someone at the door.

examples.means: There's an open door.
examples.literal: There is a door open.

examples.means: Is there coffee?
examples.literal: There is coffee?

contrasts.says: Use hay to introduce what is there; use estar to locate something already identified: El café está aquí.

mistakes.why: puerta is feminine, so use una. hay stays the same.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons 21–40, open to correction.

adjective-after.explain: A descriptive adjective often follows its noun: una puerta abierta, an open door. It agrees with the noun: abierto with carro, abierta with puerta. Other placements can be grammatical and can change emphasis or meaning; noun first is the useful pattern here.
adjective-after.why: English puts open before door. Spanish puts it after here: una puerta [[abierta]]. The -a matches the feminine noun puerta.

examples.means: There's an open door.
examples.literal: There is a door open.

examples.means: I walk to the open door.
examples.literal: I walk to the door open.

contrasts.says: The position and the ending are separate: abierta follows puerta and agrees with it.
In La puerta está abierta, abierta describes a state after estar; it is not part of the noun phrase la puerta abierta.

mistakes.why: abierta agrees with feminine puerta.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons 21–40, open to correction.

question-word.explain: Use qué for what, quién for who, dónde for where and cómo for how. They ask for the missing part of an answer and carry written accents. Spanish does not add do or does. A preposition may come before the question word when the construction needs it. The verb often follows the question word, but this is not a ban on other natural Spanish orders.
question-word.why: In [[¿Cómo]] puedo ayudar?, you are asking how to help. In [[¿Dónde]] está tu amigo?, the missing information is the place.

examples.means: How can I help?
examples.literal: How I can help?

examples.means: Where's your friend?
examples.literal: Where is your friend?

examples.means: What can your friend do?
examples.literal: What can do your friend?

contrasts.says: A yes-or-no question asks whether something is true; a question word asks for a person, place, thing or other missing information.

mistakes.why: The question word does not change the rule after puedo: use the infinitive ayudar.
The subject tu amigo takes está, not the tú form estás.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons 21–40, open to correction.

personal-a.explain: With verbs such as ayudar, a specific person as the direct object normally takes a before them: Ayudo a mi amigo. This a does not mean that anyone is moving toward the person. Do not copy it automatically to things or to every verb with a person; learn the verb and its construction.
personal-a.why: In Ayudo [[a mi amigo]], mi amigo is the person receiving the help. English says help my friend without a word for this a.

examples.text: Ayudo a mi amigo con el carro.
examples.means: I'm helping my friend with the car.
examples.literal: I help to my friend with the car.

examples.text: Ayudo a tu mamá en casa.
examples.means: I help your mom at home.
examples.literal: I help to your mom at home.

contrasts.says: Spanish uses personal a in these sentences; English help takes the person directly.
mi and tu still describe whose friend or parent it is; a goes before the whole phrase.

mistakes.why: The subject yo requires ayudo. Personal a does not change the verb ending.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons 21–40, open to correction.

progressive.explain: Use a form of estar followed by the gerund to present an action in progress: Estoy buscando mi llave. For buscar the gerund is buscando; it does not change for the person or for gender. estar changes: estoy, estás, está, están. Spanish also uses its simple present for many situations where English uses an -ing form.
progressive.why: [[Estoy buscando]] makes the search an action in progress. Change who is searching and only estar changes: [[Estás buscando]].

examples.means: Today I'm looking for my key.
examples.literal: Today I am looking for my key.

examples.means: Are you looking in the car?
examples.literal: Are you looking in the car?

examples.means: They're looking for the key.
examples.literal: They are looking for the key.

contrasts.says: Ellos vienen hoy uses the simple present for an arranged arrival today; an English -ing does not automatically require the Spanish progressive.
After puedo use buscar; after estoy for an ongoing action use buscando.

mistakes.why: estar must agree with yo.
The plural subject ellos takes están; buscando stays unchanged.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons 21–40, open to correction.

plural.explain: For common nouns ending in a vowel, add -s: cita becomes citas, hora becomes horas. Many nouns ending in a consonant add -es; a final z changes to c before that ending. The article and describing words agree with the noun, and a plural subject takes a plural verb. Feminine plural nouns take las rather than la.
plural.why: Two appointments are dos [[citas]]. As a subject they take a plural verb: [[Las citas son]] a las dos.

examples.means: I have two appointments today.
examples.literal: I have two appointments today.

examples.text: Tengo una cita en dos horas.
examples.means: I have an appointment in two hours.
examples.literal: I have an appointment in two hours.

examples.text: Las citas son a las dos.
examples.means: The appointments are at two o'clock.
examples.literal: The appointments are at the two.

contrasts.says: Gender stays the same in the plural: cita and citas are feminine.
hay itself does not become plural: Hay dos citas.

mistakes.why: After dos, use the plural citas.

mistakes.wrong: Las citas es a las dos.
mistakes.right: Las citas son a las dos.
mistakes.why: The plural subject las citas takes son.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons 21–40, open to correction.

contractions.explain: a and de join the masculine singular article el in ordinary noun phrases: a + el becomes al, de + el becomes del. They do not join la, las or los. The pronoun él, meaning he or him, is different from the article and stays separate. In ver al doctor the a is personal a, joined to the article el.
contractions.why: Keep the personal a and the article, but write them together: ver [[al]] doctor.

examples.means: I want to see the doctor.
examples.literal: I want to see to the doctor.

examples.text: Quiero ver al doctor en una hora.
examples.means: I want to see the doctor in an hour.
examples.literal: I want to see to the doctor in an hour.

contrasts.says: ver al doctor includes personal a before the doctor; ver la puerta has no personal a.
del combines de with el. With mi, keep de separate: la puerta de mi carro.

mistakes.why: a and the article el contract to al.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons 21–40, open to correction.

time-telling.explain: To tell the time, use es la una for one o'clock and son las with other hours: Son las dos. To say when something happens, use a la una or a las dos. The feminine articles refer to hours. An appointment remains singular even if its time contains las: Mi cita es a las dos.
time-telling.why: [[Son las dos]] answers what time it is. Mi cita es [[a las dos]] tells when the appointment is. The a makes it at two.

examples.means: It's two o'clock.
examples.literal: Are the two.

examples.text: Mi cita es a las dos.
examples.means: My appointment is at two o'clock.
examples.literal: My appointment is at the two.

examples.text: A las dos tengo que trabajar.
examples.means: At two o'clock I have to work.
examples.literal: At the two I have to work.

contrasts.says: Use ser to tell the time and to say when an appointment is.
las agrees with the understood plural hours; it does not make mi cita plural.

mistakes.why: Use the plural article las for two o'clock.

mistakes.wrong: Mi cita son a las dos.
mistakes.right: Mi cita es a las dos.
mistakes.why: Here the subject is singular mi cita, so the verb is es.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons 21–40, open to correction.

prepositional-pronoun.explain: contigo means with you when addressing one person as tú. It is one word, used after the verb or wherever the with-you phrase belongs: Quiero estar contigo. More generally, many prepositions take mí and ti; with con the forms are conmigo and contigo. Pronouns such as él, ella and usted keep their form after a preposition.
prepositional-pronoun.why: The con is already inside [[contigo]]. There is no separate con before it: Quiero estar [[contigo]].

examples.means: I want to be with you.
examples.literal: I want to be with you.

examples.means: I can be with you now.
examples.literal: I can be with you now.

examples.means: This is for you.
examples.literal: This is for you.

contrasts.says: tú is used as a subject; contigo is the with-you phrase.
To someone you address as usted, use con usted. contigo belongs to tú.

mistakes.why: With con, the familiar singular you is contigo, not tú.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons 21–40, open to correction.

imperative.explain: Use a command form to ask or tell someone to act. With one person you address as tú, llamar gives llama: Llama al doctor, por favor. Many regular affirmative tú commands look like the él or ella present form, but common irregular commands must be learned. A subject word is usually unnecessary. Object pronouns attach to affirmative commands; negative commands use a different form, taught later.
imperative.why: [[Llama]] addresses the listener and asks for action. por favor makes the request polite without changing the familiar tú command.

examples.means: Call the doctor, please.
examples.literal: Call to the doctor, please.

examples.means: Call your mom.
examples.literal: Call to your mom.

contrasts.says: llama can also be a present-tense statement about someone else. The situation, subject and intonation distinguish the request.
Adding por favor does not turn a tú command into an usted command; the verb form must change for usted.

mistakes.why: An explicit tú requires the tú command llama, not the usted command llame.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons 21–40, open to correction.

pronoun-attached.explain: An object pronoun can attach to an infinitive: ayudar plus me becomes ayudarme, to help me. With poder and an infinitive, it can instead go before the conjugated verb: Me puedes ayudar. It does not go between puedes and ayudar. Pronouns also attach to affirmative commands and can attach to gerunds; add a written accent when the spelling rules require it.
pronoun-attached.why: In ¿Puedes [[ayudarme]]?, me is the person receiving the help. The infinitive and its pronoun are written together; English keeps help me as two words.

examples.means: Can you help me now?
examples.literal: You can help me now?

examples.means: Do you have a moment to help me?
examples.literal: You have a moment for to help me?

contrasts.says: The verb remains an infinitive after puedes: ayudarme contains ayudar, not a conjugated form.
Before a conjugated verb the pronoun is separate; on an infinitive it is attached.

mistakes.why: yo is a subject pronoun. The person helped is me, attached here to ayudar.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons 21–40, open to correction.

reflexive.explain: Some verbs are learned with a pronoun that matches the subject. quedarse means to stay: me quedo for I stay, te quedas for you stay. The pronoun is required for this use. It does not literally mean that you do an action to yourself; pronominal verbs can have their own meanings. Both the pronoun and the verb form follow the person.
reflexive.why: In [[me quedo]], me goes with the first-person form quedo. In [[te quedas]], te goes with the tú form quedas. Learn each pair together.

examples.text: Esta noche me quedo en casa.
examples.means: I'm staying home tonight.
examples.literal: Tonight myself I stay at home.

examples.means: Are you staying here too?
examples.literal: Yourself you stay here too?

contrasts.says: The pronoun in quedarse belongs to the verb and refers back to its subject; an ordinary object can refer to another person.
me and te do not replace the ending. The ending still changes for the subject.

mistakes.why: yo requires quedo.
tú requires quedas.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons 21–40, open to correction.

verb-preposition.explain: Do not copy an English verb's preposition automatically. esperar means wait or wait for: Esperamos al doctor. When the person awaited is specific, personal a comes before that person, and a plus el becomes al. For a length of waiting, use hasta for the endpoint: Esperamos hasta las tres. Other verbs have their own patterns to learn.
verb-preposition.why: English uses wait for the doctor. Spanish uses esperamos [[al doctor]]: that a marks the person as an object; it is not a translation of for.

examples.means: We're waiting here for the doctor.
examples.literal: We wait for here to the doctor.

examples.means: I'm waiting for my friend.
examples.literal: I wait for to my friend.

examples.means: We're waiting until three o'clock.
examples.literal: We wait until the three.

contrasts.says: The a before a specific person is personal a.
The a and the article el combine: al doctor. There is no contraction in a mi amiga.

mistakes.why: Personal a combines with the article el.
The verb still agrees with its subject yo.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons 21–40, open to correction.

object-pronoun.explain: me means me and te means you when that person is the object of a verb: ¿Me oyes?, Te oigo. These little pronouns go before a conjugated verb in ordinary present-tense statements and questions. With no, put no before the pronoun: No te oigo. The verb ending identifies the person hearing; the pronoun identifies the person heard. These same forms can also mark a recipient, depending on the verb.
object-pronoun.why: [[Te]] oigo means I hear you: te is you, and oigo says I hear. [[Me]] oyes reverses the roles: you hear me.

examples.means: Can you hear me?
examples.literal: Me you hear?

examples.means: I can hear you again.
examples.literal: You I hear again.

examples.means: I can't hear you.
examples.literal: Not you I hear.

examples.means: She can hear me again.
examples.literal: She me hears again.

contrasts.says: In me quedo, the pronoun belongs to quedarse and refers to its subject. In me oyes, me is the person that you hear.
With an infinitive, a pronoun can attach to the end: ayudarme. It is separate before oyes or oigo.

mistakes.why: oigo agrees with the subject yo. te is the object, not the subject.
oyes agrees with the subject tú. me is the person heard.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons 21–40, open to correction.

because.explain: porque joins an action or statement to its reason. Each clause keeps the verb form its subject needs: Comemos ahora porque tenemos que trabajar. The subjects need not be the same: Espero aquí porque el doctor está ocupado. Spanish often leaves out a subject already clear from the verb or context. porque is written as one word without an accent. It differs from the two-word accented question por qué, introduced later.
because.why: The reason begins with [[porque]]. In Me quedo en cama porque quiero dormir, [[quiero]] is the conjugated verb and dormir is the infinitive after it.

examples.text: Me quedo en cama porque quiero dormir.
examples.means: I'm staying in bed because I want to sleep.
examples.literal: Myself I stay in bed because I want to sleep.

examples.text: Comemos ahora porque tenemos que trabajar.
examples.means: We're eating now because we have to work.
examples.literal: We eat now because we have to work.

examples.text: Espero aquí porque el doctor está ocupado.
examples.means: I'm waiting here because the doctor is busy.
examples.literal: I wait here because the doctor is busy.

contrasts.says: Inside a reason clause, querer or tener que still takes an infinitive: quiero dormir, tenemos que trabajar.
The ending can identify the subject in both clauses; porque does not require yo or nosotros.

mistakes.wrong: Comemos ahora porque tenemos que trabajamos.
mistakes.right: Comemos ahora porque tenemos que trabajar.
mistakes.why: After tenemos que, use the infinitive trabajar.

mistakes.wrong: Espero aquí porque el doctor están ocupado.
mistakes.right: Espero aquí porque el doctor está ocupado.
mistakes.why: The singular subject el doctor takes está.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons 41–60, open to correction.

negative-concord.explain: Use no before the verb when nada, nadie, nunca or a ningún phrase follows it in the negative statements here: No tengo nada, No conozco a nadie, No tomo café nunca, No tengo ningún libro aquí. The negatives reinforce one negative meaning; they do not cancel each other. When the negative word comes before the verb, it supplies the negation itself: Nadie quiere trabajar hoy, Nunca compro comida aquí. nadie means nobody and takes a singular verb as subject. ningún is the shortened form of ninguno before a masculine singular noun. With no, English often chooses any or anyone, while Spanish keeps its negative word.
negative-concord.why: In No tengo [[nada]], no and nada work together. Move a negative word before the verb and it supplies the negative itself: [[Nadie]] quiere trabajar hoy.

examples.means: I don't have any money at all.
examples.literal: Not I have nothing of money.

examples.means: I don't know anyone here.
examples.literal: Not I know to nobody here.

examples.means: Nobody wants to work today.
examples.literal: Nobody wants to work today.

contrasts.says: no also negates an ordinary noun phrase without nada or nadie. Negative concord explains what happens when a negative word joins it.
nadie still takes personal a as the object of conocer: No conozco a nadie aquí.

mistakes.why: The masculine singular ningún requires singular libro.
nadie as the subject takes third-person singular quiere, not first-person quiero.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons 41–60, open to correction.

que-clause.explain: Creo que introduces what the speaker thinks: Creo que podemos comer aquí. The first verb has its own subject, I; the following clause has another, we. que is written without an accent and links the clauses. English may omit that, but the Spanish taught here keeps que. Affirmative statements with creo que normally use the indicative: vive, es, podemos. This is a content clause, not a question. Other contexts, including negated beliefs and wishes, can require other mood choices; those come later.
que-clause.why: Creo [[que]] mi amiga vive aquí has a complete thought after que: [[mi amiga vive aquí]]. The verb vive agrees with mi amiga, independently of creo.

examples.means: I think we can eat here.
examples.literal: I think that we can eat here.

examples.text: Creo que mi amiga vive aquí.
examples.means: I think my friend lives here.
examples.literal: I think that my friend lives here.

examples.means: Do you think this book is good?
examples.literal: You think that this book is good?

contrasts.says: Unaccented que joins clauses. Accented qué asks what or which.
In creo que podemos comer, podemos is conjugated and comer remains the infinitive required by poder.

mistakes.wrong: Creo que mi amiga vives aquí.
mistakes.right: Creo que mi amiga vive aquí.
mistakes.why: mi amiga requires the singular third-person vive.

mistakes.wrong: Yo crees que podemos comer aquí.
mistakes.right: Yo creo que podemos comer aquí.
mistakes.why: yo requires creo; the next clause still uses podemos for we.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons 41–60, open to correction.

indirect-object.explain: When someone gives or tells something, the indirect object names its recipient. In Mi mamá me cuenta una historia, mi mamá is the subject, una historia is what is told, and me is the person receiving the story. Before the conjugated verb, write me, te or le separately. With an infinitive the pronoun can attach: contarte, contarle. le can mean to him, to her or to formal you. An a phrase can name the same recipient explicitly: Él le cuenta algo a mi amiga. Here le and a mi amiga refer to the same person, not to two different recipients. More pronouns and combinations are introduced later.
indirect-object.why: Mi mamá [[me]] cuenta una historia tells us who hears the story. In Él [[le]] cuenta algo [[a mi amiga]], the full a phrase explains who le means.

examples.text: Mi mamá me cuenta una historia.
examples.means: My mom is telling me a story.
examples.literal: My mom to me tells a story.

examples.text: ¿Puedes contarle una historia a mi mamá?
examples.means: Can you tell my mom a story?
examples.literal: You can tell to her a story to my mom?

examples.text: Él le cuenta algo a mi amiga.
examples.means: He tells my friend something.
examples.literal: He to her tells something to my friend.

contrasts.says: me and te have the same forms as direct objects. The verb and its construction tell us their role: the recipient of a story is indirect.
The a naming a recipient is not the personal a of a human direct object. In contarle una historia a mi mamá, the story is the direct object.
The recipient pronoun can attach to contar: contarte or contarle. Before cuenta it is a separate word.

mistakes.wrong: Mi mamá me cuentan una historia.
mistakes.right: Mi mamá me cuenta una historia.
mistakes.why: The subject mi mamá is singular. The recipient me does not control the verb ending.

mistakes.wrong: ¿Puedes contarle un historia a mi mamá?
mistakes.right: ¿Puedes contarle una historia a mi mamá?
mistakes.why: historia is feminine and requires una.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons 41–60, open to correction.

gustar.explain: gustar describes something as pleasing to someone. In Me gusta quedarme en casa, me names the person who likes it and the infinitive activity quedarme en casa is the grammatical subject. One thing or one infinitive activity takes gusta. Plural things take gustan: Me gustan las películas divertidas. te names a familiar singular listener. With quedarse, the attached pronoun also identifies who stays: quedarme for me, quedarte for you. Thus ¿Te gusta quedarte en casa? asks whether you like staying at home. The plural verb does not count the people who like something; it agrees with the things liked.
gustar.why: [[Me]] gusta quedarme en casa names the experiencer. The subject is the activity, so use [[gusta]]. With las películas, use [[gustan]].

examples.means: I like staying at home.
examples.literal: To me is pleasing to stay at home.

examples.means: Do you like staying at home?
examples.literal: To you is pleasing to stay at home?

examples.means: I like fun movies.
examples.literal: To me are pleasing the movies fun.

contrasts.says: The experiencer uses the same kind of pronoun as a recipient: me or te here.
In Me gusta quedarme en casa, the first me belongs to gustar. The me attached to quedar belongs to quedarse.
gustar still has subject agreement, but the grammatical subject is what is liked, unlike English I like.

mistakes.why: The infinitive activity takes singular gusta.
películas is feminine plural, so its article is las.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons 41–60, open to correction.

ir-a.explain: Use a conjugated form of ir, then a, then an infinitive to express a plan or prediction: Voy a traer agua para todos. ir supplies the person: voy for I, vas for familiar you, vamos for we. The infinitive does not change its ending for that person. The construction can include ir again: Voy a ir a la cocina por agua. The first voy a introduces the plan; the infinitive ir describes going somewhere. ir followed directly by a place, as in Voy al parque, describes movement rather than this infinitive construction.
ir-a.why: [[Voy a traer]] describes a plan. Change the subject to we and the first verb changes: [[Vamos a traer]]. traer stays an infinitive.

examples.text: Voy a traer agua para todos.
examples.means: I'm going to bring water for everyone.
examples.literal: I go to bring water for everyone.

examples.means: Are you going to bring coffee too?
examples.literal: You go to bring coffee too?

examples.text: Vamos a traer agua de la cocina.
examples.means: We're going to bring water from the kitchen.
examples.literal: We go to bring water from the kitchen.

contrasts.says: Both ir a and poder use an infinitive for the following action, but ir a requires a.
When a precedes the article el it becomes al. The a before an infinitive is separate.

mistakes.wrong: Voy a traigo agua para todos.
mistakes.right: Voy a traer agua para todos.
mistakes.why: The verb after voy a is the infinitive traer.

mistakes.wrong: Vamos a traemos agua de la cocina.
mistakes.right: Vamos a traer agua de la cocina.
mistakes.why: vamos already carries we; use infinitive traer after a.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons 41–60, open to correction.

por-para.explain: English for has several Spanish equivalents. para can name who something is intended for: agua para todos, leche para mi mamá. It can also introduce a purpose with an infinitive, as in tiempo para comer. por has other uses, including the thing someone goes to get: ir por café. In Voy a ir a la cocina por agua, the kitchen is the destination and water is what the speaker will get there. The familiar question por qué asks for a reason. These are uses to learn in context, not an exhaustive rule for every por or para. Some verbs need neither word where English uses for, such as esperar.
por-para.why: Agua [[para todos]] identifies the recipients. Ir [[por café]] describes fetching coffee. The meaning comes from the full construction.

examples.text: Voy a traer agua para todos.
examples.means: I'm going to bring water for everyone.
examples.literal: I go to bring water for everyone.

examples.text: Voy a ir a la cocina por agua.
examples.means: I'm going to go to the kitchen for water.
examples.literal: I go to go to the kitchen for water.

examples.means: Do you want to go get coffee?
examples.literal: You want to go for coffee?

contrasts.says: Learn a verb with its complement. Spanish esperar takes its object directly, plus personal a where needed; English wait for does not force por or para.
porque introduces a reason clause. por qué is the question why; por alone has several other uses.

mistakes.why: querer takes an infinitive here; the fetching expression is ir por café.

mistakes.wrong: Hay agua para todos en el mesa.
mistakes.right: Hay agua para todos en la mesa.
mistakes.why: mesa is feminine. para todos does not affect the article of mesa.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons 41–60, open to correction.

past.explain: The preterite presents an event as completed. It can describe yesterday or a completed event today: Ayer llamé al doctor, Hoy trabajé en casa. Regular -ar verbs have -é for I and -aste for familiar you: trabajé, trabajaste. The third-person singular ending is -ó: llamó. Written accents matter in these forms. hacer is irregular: hice for I and hiciste for tú. Learn those forms with their verb. Spanish usually leaves out a subject that the ending or context already supplies. This lesson begins with completed events; later lessons contrast the preterite with ongoing or habitual past background.
past.why: [[Trabajé]] says I worked, while [[trabajaste]] says you worked. A time word such as hoy does not force another tense: Hoy trabajé en casa presents the work as completed.

examples.means: I worked at home today.
examples.literal: Today I worked at home.

examples.means: Did you work yesterday?
examples.literal: You worked yesterday?

examples.means: I made coffee for my mom.
examples.literal: I made coffee for my mom.

contrasts.says: trabajo and other present forms describe the present or a routine. trabajé presents a completed event in the past.
hice already identifies I. Add a subject word only when useful for contrast or clarity.

mistakes.why: yo takes first-person trabajé, not the tú form trabajaste.
An explicit tú cannot be the subject of hice. The tú form is hiciste; the subject can be omitted.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons 41–60, open to correction.

perfect.explain: The present perfect combines present haber with a past participle: he comido, has tomado. he identifies I and has identifies familiar you. Regular participles include -ado for -ar verbs and -ido for many -er and -ir verbs: comprado, comido. visto is irregular, and leído needs its written accent. With haber, the participle does not change for gender or number. This tense can connect an event to the present, report experience, or describe what has happened up to now. The preterite presents a completed event: Ayer comí en casa y tomé café. Usage varies across Latin America and elsewhere: hoy can occur with either tense, and the presence of ya does not force one tense. Do not translate every English have done mechanically.
perfect.why: In [[he comido]], haber carries the person and comido is unchanged. In [[has tomado]], the subject is familiar you. The past forms comí and tomé do not follow haber.

examples.means: What have you eaten today?
examples.literal: What you have eaten today?

examples.means: Have you had enough water yet?
examples.literal: Already you have drunk enough water?

examples.text: Ayer comí en casa y tomé café.
examples.means: Yesterday I ate at home and had coffee.
examples.literal: Yesterday I ate at home and I had coffee.

contrasts.says: The preterite comí is a conjugated verb by itself. In he comido, he is conjugated and comido is a participle. Regional and contextual preferences affect which tense a speaker chooses.
No he comido nada keeps no before the auxiliary and nada after the participle. Together they express one negative.

mistakes.why: After haber use participle comido, not preterite comí.
After has use the participle leído, not present leo.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons 41–60, open to correction.

double-object.explain: When both the thing and its recipient are object pronouns, put the recipient first. In Se lo llevo a mi hermano, lo replaces a masculine singular thing such as el libro. The recipient would be le by itself, but le becomes se immediately before lo. The same change applies to les before lo, la, los or las. se here identifies a recipient; it is not the reflexive se of llamarse. The phrase a mi hermano tells us who the recipient is. se alone does not reveal the recipient's gender or number. The pair stays together: before a conjugated verb, or attached together when a construction allows attachment. This lesson practices the position before the conjugated verb.
double-object.why: In [[se lo llevo]], [[se]] is the recipient and [[lo]] is the thing taken. In ¿Le das el libro?, only the recipient is a pronoun. Replace el libro with lo and le changes to se: Sí, [[se lo doy]].

examples.text: Se lo llevo a mi hermano.
examples.means: I'm taking it to my brother.
examples.literal: To him it I take to my brother.

examples.text: No se lo llevo a mi mamá todavía.
examples.means: I'm not taking it to my mom yet.
examples.literal: Not to her it I take to my mom yet.

examples.text: ¿Le das el libro? Sí, se lo doy.
examples.means: Are you giving him the book? Yes, I'm giving it to him.
examples.literal: To him you give the book? Yes, to him it I give.

contrasts.says: le is possible before das when the direct object is the noun el libro. It becomes se when that object is replaced by lo.
In se llama, se belongs to llamarse. In se lo llevo, se identifies the recipient of the book.
lo agrees with the masculine singular thing replaced; it does not identify who receives it.

mistakes.wrong: Le lo llevo a mi hermano.
mistakes.right: Se lo llevo a mi hermano.
mistakes.why: Before lo, le changes to se.

mistakes.wrong: Lo se llevo a mi hermano.
mistakes.right: Se lo llevo a mi hermano.
mistakes.why: The recipient se precedes the direct object lo.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons 61–80, open to correction.

subjunctive.explain: The present subjunctive supplies the forms for negative tú commands and for both positive and negative usted and ustedes commands. Compare the affirmative tú command tira with no tires. For regular -ar verbs, the negative tú ending is -es, and the usted/ustedes endings are -e/-en: tires, agarre, agarren. Regular -er and -ir verbs use -as for negative tú and -a/-an for usted/ustedes. Irregular stems must be learned with the verb: poner gives no pongas, ponga and pongan, while affirmative tú is pon. Use no before any object pronouns in a negative command: No lo pongas en la mesa. Pronouns attach to affirmative commands; they are separate before negative commands. usted addresses one person formally; ustedes addresses more than one person in the Spanish taught here. The subjunctive has other uses, but this lesson practices commands only.
subjunctive.why: [[No tires]] addresses tú. [[Ponga]] addresses usted, and [[pongan]] addresses ustedes. The negative word changes the tú command form; it does not change which form an usted or ustedes command uses.

examples.text: No tires ese libro, por favor.
examples.means: Don't throw that book, please.
examples.literal: Not throw that book, please.

examples.text: Ponga el teléfono en el sofá, por favor.
examples.means: Put the phone on the sofa, please. (formal)
examples.literal: Put the phone on the sofa, please.

examples.text: Pongan la llave en la mesa.
examples.means: You all, put the key on the table.
examples.literal: Put the key on the table.

examples.text: No lo pongas en la mesa.
examples.means: Don't put it on the table.
examples.literal: Not it put on the table.

examples.means: Do not put the book here. (formal)
examples.literal: Not put the book here.

contrasts.says: An affirmative tú command can have a different form: pon versus no pongas. The imperative idea describes the instruction; this idea explains the subjunctive forms used for some instructions.
Affirmative commands attach object pronouns. Negative commands place the pronouns before the verb, after no.
The command form distinguishes familiar singular tú, formal singular usted and plural ustedes.

mistakes.wrong: No lo pongas en el mesa.
mistakes.right: No lo pongas en la mesa.
mistakes.why: mesa is feminine. The pronoun lo replaces a different object, not mesa.

mistakes.wrong: Ponga el teléfono en la sofá, por favor.
mistakes.right: Ponga el teléfono en el sofá, por favor.
mistakes.why: sofá is masculine, so use el sofá.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons 61–80, open to correction.

tener.explain: Spanish expresses age with tener and a number of years. In Mi hijo tiene cuatro años, tiene agrees with mi hijo; cuatro años is the age. English uses be instead: My son is four years old. Ask ¿Cuántos años tiene tu hijo? to ask his age. cuántos is masculine plural to agree with años. The number does not control the verb: one child still takes tiene even with plural años. The same construction can give the age of an object: Ese libro ya tiene cuatro años. tener also belongs to learned expressions for physical states, but this lesson practices age.
tener.why: [[Mi hijo tiene]] identifies whose age is given. [[Cuatro años]] states the age. In ¿[[Cuántos años]] tiene tu hijo?, both words are plural.

examples.means: How old is your son?
examples.literal: How many years has your son?

examples.means: My son is four years old.
examples.literal: My son has four years.

examples.text: Ese libro ya tiene cuatro años.
examples.means: That book is already four years old.
examples.literal: That book already has four years.

contrasts.says: English be in an age expression is expressed with tener, rather than by selecting ser or estar.
Use años after a number greater than one. The subject still determines whether the verb is singular or plural.

mistakes.why: Four years requires plural años.
cuántos and años are both masculine plural.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons 61–80, open to correction.

quantity.explain: When the conversation has identified a countable noun, a number can stand for it without repeating the noun: ¿Necesitas libros? Tengo dos. Spanish does not need an extra word meaning of them. For one, use uno with a masculine noun understood and una with a feminine noun understood. Compare un libro with Tengo uno, and una foto with Tengo una. For none, use ninguno or ninguna. Before a masculine singular noun, ninguno shortens to ningún; standing alone, it keeps the final -o. A negative quantity after the verb needs preceding negation: No tengo ninguno. Here each example supplies the noun so the reference is clear.
quantity.why: In ¿Quieres un libro? Tengo [[uno]], uno replaces libro. With foto, use [[una]]. In ¿Tienes fotos? No tengo [[ninguna]], ninguna agrees with the understood feminine noun.

examples.means: Do you need books? I have two.
examples.literal: You need books? I have two.

examples.means: Do you want a book? I have one.
examples.literal: You want a book? I have one.

examples.means: Do you want a photo? I have one.
examples.literal: You want a photo? I have one.

examples.means: Do you have books? I don't have any.
examples.literal: You have books? Not I have any.

examples.means: Do you have photos? I don't have any.
examples.literal: You have photos? Not I have any.

contrasts.says: No tengo ninguna keeps no before the verb because ninguna follows it.
uno and ninguno are masculine; una and ninguna are feminine. Match the noun understood.
dos can replace plural libros without repeating it. uno replaces a singular libro.

mistakes.wrong: No tengo ningún libros. Mi hermano tiene uno.
mistakes.right: No tengo ningún libro. Mi hermano tiene uno.
mistakes.why: Before a noun, ningún requires the masculine singular libro.

mistakes.wrong: No tengo ninguna fotos. Mi mamá tiene una.
mistakes.right: No tengo ninguna foto. Mi mamá tiene una.
mistakes.why: ninguna requires the singular foto in this construction.

source.note: Written with the Spanish lessons 61–80, open to correction.

infinitive-clause.explain: An infinitive can name an activity rather than give a command or state who performs it. In Manejar es importante para mi trabajo, the activity manejar is the subject of es. The verb is singular when one activity is described. The same pattern can put the activity later: Es importante manejar. A preposition can connect an infinitive to a noun or adjective, but the construction determines which one. tiempo para comer describes time for an activity. Su historia es difícil de entender describes a story that is hard to understand: the story is what someone would understand. Compare Es difícil entender esa historia, where the whole action entender esa historia is described as difficult. Keep the verb after the preposition in its infinitive form. Do not translate every English to with a; aprender a manejar, tiempo para comer and difícil de entender have different links.
infinitive-clause.why: [[Manejar]] names an activity and takes singular [[es]]. In tiempo [[para comer]], para introduces the purpose. In difícil [[de entender]], de belongs to the construction describing the thing understood.

examples.text: Manejar es importante para mi trabajo.
examples.means: Driving is important for my job.
examples.literal: To drive is important for my job.

examples.text: ¿Por qué es tan importante aprender a manejar?
examples.means: Why is learning to drive so important?
examples.literal: For what is so important to learn to drive?

examples.means: I have time to eat.
examples.literal: I have time for to eat.

examples.text: Su historia es difícil de entender.
examples.means: Her story is hard to understand.
examples.literal: Her story is difficult of to understand.

contrasts.says: In quiero manejar, querer requires the infinitive for the desired action. In Manejar es importante, the infinitive itself is the subject.
para can express a purpose with an infinitive. It does not replace a or de in every construction.
Learn the connecting word with its construction: aprender a, tiempo para, difícil de.

mistakes.why: Use infinitive comer after para in this purpose expression.

mistakes.wrong: Su historia es difícil de entiendo.
mistakes.right: Su historia es difícil de entender.
mistakes.why: Use infinitive entender after de in this construction.
